q: You read the wind instruments before leaving the anchorage. What force is the mean wind?
a: Force 6
o: Force 4
Force 5
Force 7
why: F6 is 22–27 kn; the force is named from the mean wind, not the gusts.

fig.title: Wind instruments
lines: True wind 25 kn, steady for an hour

q: You look out from the harbour wall before deciding whether to go. Roughly what wind is blowing outside?
a: F7, 28–33 knots
o: F4, 11–16 knots
F5, 17–21 knots
F10, 48–55 knots
why: Sea heaping up with foam blown in streaks along the wind is the Beaufort picture of F7.

fig.title: Outside the breakwater
lines: is blown in streaks along the wind

q: You see this sea from the cockpit before leaving. How do you set the sails of your 40-ft charter yacht?
a: F4 — full sail, a good breeze
o: F2 — too light, motor instead
F6 — two reefs before leaving
F8 — stay in harbour
why: Small waves with fairly frequent white horses is F4, 11–16 kn: full sail on a 40-footer.

q: You are close-hauled under full main and genoa. The boat heels hard and fights the helm. What do you do?
a: Reef now, before the wind builds further
o: Wait for force 7, then reef
Sheet the main in harder to cut the heeling
Luff up and hold her there for an hour
why: Reef early — the first time you think of it, and well before F6 on a charter yacht.

fig.note: True wind rising 16 → 20 kn, weather helm

q: You have been running pleasantly under full sail for two hours. Now you must turn and beat back to harbour. What do you expect?
a: Much more wind and spray — reef first
o: The same wind, just from ahead
Less wind, as you will be sailing slower
A lighter wind — shake out any reef
why: Downwind your boat speed is subtracted from the true wind; upwind it is added.

fig.note: Running · apparent wind 13 kn, sea easy

q: You log the wind every hour. What is the true wind now, and what force do you write in the log?
a: About 21 kn — F5
o: About 14 kn — F4
About 7 kn — F3
About 28 kn — F7
why: Dead downwind, true wind = apparent wind + boat speed: 14 + 7 = 21 kn, top of F5.

q: You plan a day sail with a family crew. What do you set the boat up for?
a: The gusts — reef to handle 30 kn
o: The mean wind — full sail for F5
The lulls — shake out reefs in them
The sea state only — the wind is fine
why: Gusts are what overpower the boat: reef for the gusts, not the mean wind.

q: The mean wind is 20 knots in open water. Under the high island ahead, gusts typically run 50 % above the mean. What do you prepare for?
a: Gusts of about 30 kn — F7 strength
o: About 20 kn — the same as outside
About 10 kn — the island shelters you
About 40 kn — double the mean wind
why: Gust factor: 20 kn × 1.5 = 30 kn, so reef for F7 gusts, not the F5 mean.

q: You are in Paros, planning to cross to Naxos tomorrow. What wind does this warning forecast?
a: 34–40 kn, locally 41–47 kn
o: 22–27 kn, locally 28–33 kn
28–33 kn, locally 34–40 kn
48–55 kn, locally 56–63 kn
why: F8 is 34–40 kn and F9 41–47 kn — a gale: stay in harbour.

q: You set full sail at 10 knots of wind this morning. By noon it blows 20 knots. How has the load on sails and rig changed?
a: About four times as much
o: About twice as much
About the same
About eight times as much
why: Wind pressure rises with the square of the wind speed: double the wind, four times the force.

q: Sailing close-hauled across the Gulf of Corinth, you see a dark ruffled patch on the water racing towards you from windward. What do you do?
a: Be ready to ease the main as the gust hits
o: Alter course away — it is a shoal patch
Nothing — it is only a current line
Ease the sheets now — it is a calm patch ahead
why: Dark, ruffled water moving towards you from windward is a gust arriving.

q: Your weather app shows the wind for this afternoon. Roughly how many knots is that?
a: About 20 knots
o: About 10 knots
About 36 knots
About 5 knots
why: 1 m/s ≈ 2 kn, so 10 m/s ≈ 19–20 kn (F5); 36 is the km/h figure.

q: This morning the wind blew from the south. Now it blows from the west. How do you describe the change?
a: It has veered — turned clockwise
o: It has backed — turned anticlockwise
It has veered — turned anticlockwise
It has backed — turned clockwise
why: Veering = clockwise shift (S → W); backing = anticlockwise.

q: You stand with your back to this wind. Where is the centre of low pressure?
a: To the south-east
o: To the north-west
To the north-east
To the south-west
why: Buys Ballot, northern hemisphere: back to the wind, the low is on your left.

q: From which direction does the wind blow where you are?
a: From the north
o: From the south
From the west
From the east
why: Northern hemisphere: wind blows clockwise round a high, so on its east side it comes from the north.

fig.note: You are east of the high

q: Which way is the wind blowing at your position on this chart?
a: From the north-west
o: From the south-east
From the north-east
From the south-west
why: Wind circulates anticlockwise round a low in the northern hemisphere, angled slightly inwards.

fig.note: You are SW of the low

q: You are south of the track of this depression. How will the wind change during the night?
a: Veer from south-west to north-west
o: Back from south-west to south-east
Stay south-west, only weaker
Back from north-west to south-west
why: With a low passing to your north, the wind veers (clockwise) as it goes by.

fig.title: Forecast
lines: Depression moving east across the Ionian
Centre passing north of you tonight

q: The depression centre will pass to the south of you, moving east. How will the wind shift as it goes by?
a: Back from south-east through east to north-east
o: Veer from south-west through west to north-west
Veer from south-east to south-west
Stay south-east and die away
why: Low passing south of you: the wind backs (anticlockwise) — the mirror of a low passing north.

fig.title: Forecast
lines: Centre to pass 60 M south of you

q: This high is forecast to sit over the Ionian for three days. What weather do you plan for?
a: Light winds, sea breezes and sun
o: Gales and heavy rain for most of the week
Fog that lasts all day long
A strong, steady northerly gale
why: Widely spaced isobars round a high: light winds and settled weather with local breezes.

q: You read this forecast before a passage. What does it tell you to expect?
a: A clockwise shift to west, F5, after 12 h
o: An anticlockwise shift to west, F5, within 6 h
Wind staying south, gusting F5, from noon
A shift to east, F5, in 6 to 12 h
why: Veering = clockwise; "later" = more than 12 hours from the time of issue.

q: You use this chart to estimate the wind at sea near the low. How does the surface wind blow relative to the isobars?
a: Nearly along them, angled in towards the low
o: Straight across them into the low
Nearly along them, angled outwards from the low
Straight out from the low centre
why: Friction turns the surface wind 10–15° across the isobars towards low pressure at sea.

q: You have watched the weather for six hours. What has just happened?
a: A warm front has passed — warm sector now
o: A cold front has passed — clearing is coming
A high has moved over you — settled weather
A sea breeze has set in — it will die tonight
why: Warm front passing: wind veers, rain eases to drizzle, temperature rises, glass steadies.

q: You are in the warm sector. What do you prepare for when this arrives?
a: A sharp veer to NW, squalls, heavy rain
o: Hours of light drizzle and thick fog
A slow back to the south, then calm
A steady rise in temperature and humidity
why: A cold front brings a sharp veer, squalls and heavy but short rain.

fig.title: Looking west
lines: A line of towering dark cloud

q: A front passed two hours ago. What do you expect for the rest of the day?
a: Gusty NW wind, showers, clear air
o: Rain and fog for many hours to come
A calm, warm and humid afternoon
The wind backing south again soon
why: Behind a cold front the air is cooler, gusty and showery, with excellent visibility.

q: This message is on the Navtex this evening. What sequence of weather do you expect overnight?
a: Thick cloud, rain, a veer, then clearing
o: A sudden squall without any cloud warning
Clear skies all night, wind steady
Two days of thick fog, then a gale
why: An occluded front brings cloud and rain like a warm front, then a veer and clearing like a cold one.

q: You see these clouds while sailing along the coast. What do they warn you of?
a: Strong wind aloft — hard gusts off the high land
o: Settled calm weather for the rest of the day
A sea breeze is about to start along the coast
Fog will form by the evening
why: Lens-shaped clouds parked over peaks show a strong airflow over the mountains: expect fall gusts in their lee.

fig.title: Over the island's mountains
lines: They stay fixed over the peaks

q: Morning in the Ionian: small white puffy clouds with flat bases form over the land and vanish in the evening. The barometer is steady. What does it mean?
a: Settled weather, sea breeze by day
o: A front arriving within the next few hours
Thunderstorms building by midday
A gale coming in tonight
why: Small fair-weather cumulus over land with a steady glass means settled weather.

q: A front passed at 14:00. What do you expect for the evening?
a: Strong gusty wind for a while
o: A calm and settled night ahead
Fog forming in the harbour
A gradual return of the rain
why: A rapid rise brings strong wind just as a rapid fall does.

q: This is the only reading you have. What does it tell you about the day ahead?
a: Little on its own — trend matters
o: A gale is on its way tonight
Settled high pressure for the next few days
Fog is likely this morning
why: The change over 3 hours matters far more than any single value.

fig.title: Barometer
lines: No earlier readings in the log

q: The forecast also says settled. What does your barometer log tell you?
a: No change on the way
o: A depression is close by
A front is due tonight
Strong wind by morning
why: A steady glass over a day supports a settled forecast.

q: You are in a sheltered harbour at 08:00 with 20 miles of open water to the next one. What do you do?
a: Stay in harbour and prepare the boat
o: Leave now to arrive before it hits
Leave with two reefs already tied in
Anchor off the beach outside the harbour
why: A gale within 6 hours and a fast-falling glass: stay in shelter and secure the boat.

lines: Barometer −7 hPa in the last 3 h
Next harbour 20 M across open water

q: By when should you expect the gale to arrive?
a: Within 6 hours
o: In 6 to 12 hours
After 12 hours
In 24 to 48 hours
why: Imminent < 6 h, soon 6–12 h, later > 12 h from the time of issue.

q: Between what times do you expect force 7?
a: Between 14:00 and 20:00
o: Before 14:00
After 20:00
Not until tomorrow afternoon
why: "Soon" means 6 to 12 hours from the time of issue.

q: You plan to leave at 06:00 tomorrow for a five-hour passage. How does this forecast affect you?
a: F6 may arrive at any time on passage
o: F6 will have passed before you leave
F6 comes this evening, then eases
F6 is not due for two days
why: "Later" means more than 12 hours after issue — 06:00 tomorrow onward, right in your passage.

q: The forecast says visibility moderate. Can you expect to see a headland 4 miles away?
a: Probably — moderate is 2 to 5 miles
o: No — moderate is under 1000 m
No — moderate is 1000 m to 2 miles
Yes — moderate is over 10 miles
why: Visibility: good > 5 M, moderate 2–5 M, poor 1000 m–2 M, fog < 1000 m.

q: The forecast for the northern Adriatic tomorrow morning gives visibility "fog". How far will you see?
a: Less than 1000 metres
o: 1000 metres to 2 miles
2 to 5 miles
More than 5 miles
why: In a forecast, fog means visibility under 1000 m.

q: What wave height should you expect?
a: About 2.5 to 4 metres
o: About 0.5 to 1.25 metres
About 1.25 to 2.5 metres
About 6 to 9 metres
why: Sea state: slight 0.5–1.25 m, moderate 1.25–2.5 m, rough 2.5–4 m, very rough 4–6 m.

q: You plan to pass through the Mykonos–Tinos channel this afternoon. What wind do you plan for there?
a: F7 in the channel
o: F4 to 5 everywhere
F7 only far offshore
F7 only after dark
why: "Locally" means in parts of the area — channels and capes are where it happens.

fig.title: Forecast, Cyclades
lines: N 4 to 5, locally 7 in the channels

q: You read this message at 13:00 Greek summer time (UTC+3). Until when could the gale arrive?
a: Any time before 18:00 local
o: Any time before 15:00 local
Not before 19:00 local
Not before 21:00 local
why: Navtex times are UTC: 09:00 UTC = 12:00 local; imminent = within 6 h, so by 18:00 local.

q: Your Navtex printout header reads "KB12". What kind of message is it?
a: A meteorological warning
o: A navigational warning
A routine weather forecast
A search and rescue notice
why: The second letter is the type: A navigational warning, B met warning, D SAR, E forecast.

q: You are chartering out of Split. Which service issues the official sea forecast for the Croatian coast?
a: DHMZ, the Croatian met service
o: Poseidon, the Greek model service
Météo-France
The Turkish State Met Service
why: DHMZ issues the Adriatic forecast, also read in English by the Croatian coast radio stations.

q: Sailing in the Cyclades, you want a detailed wind and wave forecast made for Greek waters. Which source do you use?
a: Poseidon (HCMR)
o: DHMZ
Météo-France
A 1° global GRIB file
why: Poseidon runs high-resolution wind and wave models for the Greek seas.

q: You are on passage from the Côte d'Azur to Corsica and hear a "BMS" announced for your area. What is it?
a: A Météo-France strong-wind warning
o: A routine five-day outlook
A navigational warning for a wreck
A marina berthing notice
why: BMS (bulletin météorologique spécial) is Météo-France's warning of strong wind or gale.

q: Why is the GRIB file so far from what you see?
a: The model smooths out the funnelling
o: GRIB files show gusts, not mean wind
The GRIB shows wind at 1000 m altitude
Your wind instruments must be faulty
why: Coarse models miss local acceleration, gusts and thunderstorms — add a margin.

q: You must decide tonight whether to cross to the next island tomorrow. Which forecast do you plan on?
a: The official gale warning
o: The GRIB — it is more detailed
An average of the two, about F6
Whichever was issued more recently
why: Official warnings include forecaster judgement and local effects; a raw GRIB does not.

q: You compare models for Thursday's passage. What does this tell you?
a: Low confidence — plan for the strong case
o: ECMWF is always right — expect 15 kn
Average them — expect about 22 kn
ICON is newest — expect exactly 30 kn
why: When models disagree, confidence is low: plan for the worst plausible case and re-check.

q: It is Monday. A GRIB file shows a perfect light-wind Saturday for your crossing back to base. How much do you rely on it?
a: Little — check again each day as it nears
o: Fully — models are good to 10 days
Not at all — GRIBs are never right
Fully, as long as the file is high-resolution
why: Forecast skill falls off with time; five days out is a trend, not a plan.

q: On channel 16 Olympia Radio announces a weather bulletin on a working channel. What do you do?
a: Switch to that channel and listen
o: Stay on 16 — it is read there
Call Olympia on 16 to ask for it
Ignore it — it is for ships only
why: Coast radio announces on Ch 16, then reads the bulletin on a working channel.

q: The Greek port police have issued a departure ban for yachts because of the wind. Your charter ends at base tomorrow. What do you do?
a: Stay in port and call the charter company
o: Leave — the ban is only advice
Leave at dawn, before the wind has built up
Leave if the crew all agree in writing
why: A port-police departure ban is binding; the charter base deals with late returns.

q: You want to leave tomorrow morning. Is this forecast enough?
a: No — get a fresh one before leaving
o: Yes — forecasts hold for three days
Yes — if the sky looks the same
No — only a TV forecast will do
why: Always check the time of issue; use the latest forecast before you go.

q: Cyclades, August. The Meltemi blows F6 most afternoons. When do you make a 15-mile upwind leg?
a: Early morning, before it builds
o: Mid-afternoon, when it is steadiest
Late afternoon, as it peaks
Any time — its strength never varies
why: The Meltemi is usually lightest early in the day and strongest in the afternoon.

q: You are sailing from Kos to Leros in July. From which direction does the Meltemi usually blow here?
a: From the north-west
o: From the north-east
From the south-east
From the south-west
why: The Meltemi is NE in the north Aegean, N in the Cyclades and NW in the Dodecanese.

q: Lavrion lies north-west of the islands you want to visit. How do you plan the week?
a: Do the upwind legs first, finish with reaches
o: Run south to Santorini, beat back at the end
Sail every leg in the afternoon breeze
Stay in Lavrion until the Meltemi stops
why: In Meltemi season, get your windward work done early so the last days are not a long beat home.

fig.title: Charter from Lavrion, 7 days
lines: Ideas: Kea, Syros, Tinos, Mykonos, Paros

q: You plan to pass through the strait at A. What do you expect?
a: F7 or more and steep seas — consider waiting
o: Less wind — the islands shelter the strait
Exactly the forecast wind and sea
Calmer water in the middle, away from the islands
why: Wind funnels and accelerates between high islands; the Kafireas Strait is notorious.

q: What kind of wind is this?
a: Cold and dry, with violent gusts
o: Warm, humid and steady from the sea
A gentle afternoon sea breeze
A long swell from a distant storm
why: The Bora is a cold NE fall wind: the mean wind may be moderate, the gusts violent.

fig.title: Forecast, northern Adriatic
lines: Gusts up to 50 kn under Velebit

q: Kvarner, clear sky. A white cloud cap sits on the Velebit mountains and the air turns cold. What is coming?
a: Bora — sudden strong NE gusts
o: Jugo — slowly rising SE wind
Maestral — a pleasant NW breeze
A warm front with steady rain
why: A cloud cap on the coastal mountains is the classic warning of the Bora.

q: Southern Croatia, October. Which wind is setting in?
a: Jugo — builds slowly, rain, big seas
o: Bora — sudden, and gone by tonight
Maestral — a pleasant fair-weather breeze
Land breeze — it eases by noon
why: The Jugo (Adriatic sirocco) builds slowly with a falling glass, cloud, rain and a heavy SE sea.

fig.title: Southern Croatia, October
lines: Barometer falling slowly for a day
SE wind building, swell from the SE

q: Which wind is this?
a: Sirocco from North Africa
o: Mistral from the Rhône valley
Bora from the Dinaric Alps
Tramontana from the north
why: Sirocco: hot SE–S wind off the Sahara, humid and hazy over the sea, often carrying red dust.

fig.title: Sicily, April
lines: Red dust on the deck and sails

q: You planned to leave Marseille today for Menorca. What do you do?
a: Wait — clear sky or not, it is a gale
o: Go — a clear sky means fair weather
Go — it is a tailwind, so it is safe
Go, but keep close along the Gulf coast
why: The Mistral blows under clear skies and raises a short, steep sea in the Gulf of Lion.

q: You are at the western end of the Strait of Bonifacio when a Mistral is forecast for the Gulf of Lion. What do you expect in the strait?
a: Strong westerlies, funnelled by the strait
o: Nothing — the Mistral stays off the French coast
A light easterly as the Mistral dies
A warm southerly with heavy rain
why: The Mistral reaches Corsica and Sardinia as a westerly and funnels through the Bonifacio Strait.

q: Menorca, July. Tramontana F6 is forecast for tonight. Where do you spend the night?
a: B, on the south coast
o: A, on the north coast
C, on the east coast
Any — it is only F6
why: The Tramontana is a northerly: shelter on the south side of the island.

q: You are in Gibraltar, bound west into the Atlantic. Levante for two days, then Poniente. When do you go?
a: During the Levante — a fair wind west
o: During the Poniente — a fair wind west
Either — both blow from the south
Neither — both are night winds only
why: Levante is the easterly of the Strait, Poniente the westerly.

q: You are wintering in Malta and a Gregale 8 is forecast. From which direction must your berth be sheltered?
a: North-east
o: South-west
South-east
North-west
why: The Gregale is a strong NE wind of the central Mediterranean, notorious in Malta.

q: You are anchored in a bay on Corsica's west coast, open to the south-west. Libeccio 7 is forecast for tomorrow. What do you do?
a: Move today to shelter from the south-west
o: Stay — the Libeccio is a north-easterly
Stay — west-coast bays are sheltered from it
Wait until it arrives, then decide
why: The Libeccio is a SW wind that sends a heavy sea onto Corsica's west coast.

q: Croatia, July. Calm morning; from about 11:00 a NW breeze builds to F4 and dies at sunset. The barometer is steady. What is it?
a: Maestral — a fair-weather breeze
o: Bora — expect violent gusts from the NE
Jugo — expect rain tomorrow
A cold front — expect squalls
why: The maestral is the Adriatic's summer afternoon NW breeze, a sign of settled weather.

q: You will leave the Dardanelles into the Aegean. Which wind gives the steepest sea at the entrance?
a: A strong south-westerly
o: A strong north-easterly
A light north-easterly
A moderate northerly
why: Wind against current shortens and steepens the waves; a SW wind meets the outgoing current head-on.

fig.title: Dardanelles
lines: Surface current sets SW, out to the Aegean

q: You must reach Mykonos, to the north, by Thursday. When do you sail?
a: Wednesday, early in the morning
o: Tuesday afternoon, to get it done
Thursday morning, as it builds
Thursday afternoon, with the wind behind
why: Use the lull, and sail upwind legs early before the afternoon wind.

q: You are anchored off a hot island in summer. Yesterday afternoon the wind blew onshore. What is this light breeze?
a: A land breeze — it fades after sunrise
o: A sea breeze — it builds all morning
The Meltemi arriving early, ahead of the day
A front passing through
why: At night the land cools below the sea and air drains offshore; it dies as the sun heats the land.

fig.note: 05:00 after a clear night, wind off the land

q: What wind do you expect near the coast this afternoon?
a: Stronger — sea breeze adds to it
o: Calm — the two winds cancel out
Weaker — the land slows the wind down
Exactly F4, as forecast
why: An onshore gradient wind plus a sea breeze in the same direction gives a fresher afternoon wind.

fig.title: Forecast
lines: You are on a coast facing south-west

q: You are anchored at A. At 02:00 strong cold gusts pour down off the land. What is it, and what do you do next time?
a: Katabatic — avoid the valley mouth
o: Sea breeze — it eases after midnight
Warm front — rain follows by dawn
Jugo — it builds for two more days
why: On clear nights cold air drains down valleys and bursts out of their mouths.

q: Forecast W 5. You are about to round Cape Maleas. What do you expect?
a: More wind and a confused sea there
o: Lighter wind in the lee of the cape
Exactly the forecast wind and sea
A flat sea close under the cliffs
why: Wind accelerates round high headlands; Maleas is notorious — reef before the cape.

q: Meltemi F6. You sail in the lee of high Andros, close under the cliffs, and the wind has almost died. What do you do?
a: Stay reefed — gusts fall off the hills
o: Shake out the reefs to keep moving
Motor in closer under the cliffs
Hoist the full genoa for the light air
why: Behind high islands calm patches alternate with fierce fall gusts; stay reefed.

q: Same F6 wind across the whole gulf. Where is the sea smallest?
a: A — near the windward shore, short fetch
o: B — the waves lose energy crossing the gulf
Both the same — same wind, same sea
B — it is further from the land
why: Waves grow with the distance the wind blows over open water (the fetch).

q: You are on passage. What do you do now?
a: Reef and prepare for a violent squall
o: Keep full sail and try to outrun it
Wait for the first rain, then reef
Anchor close under the nearest high cliff
why: A cumulonimbus brings sudden gusts of 40 kn or more: reef, close hatches, lifejackets on.

fig.title: 17:00, September, Ionian
lines: Towering cloud with an anvil top

q: A thunderstorm cell is approaching against a light easterly. Just before it reaches you, what happens to the wind?
a: It drops, then a hard gust hits from the storm
o: The easterly strengthens steadily
It stays light until the rain has passed
It swings gently round to blow towards the storm
why: The cold downdraft spreads out ahead of the storm as a sudden gust front.

fig.note: Cb cell to the west, moving east

q: A thunderstorm is overhead and lightning is striking around you. Where do you keep the crew?
a: Below, clear of the mast and rigging
o: On deck, holding on to the shrouds
At the mast foot, ready to drop sail
At the stern, holding the backstay
why: Lightning follows the mast and rigging to the water; keep people below and away from metal.

q: Autumn, Ionian. A waterspout hangs under a dark cloud about two miles away. What do you do?
a: Watch its bearing and motor out of its path
o: Heave to where you are and let it pass by you
Keep your course — they never cross boats
Close up and sail nearer to watch it
why: Waterspouts can be violent; check whether its bearing is steady and move clear of its track.

q: You plan an afternoon passage. What wind do you allow for?
a: Squalls far above F3 near any storm
o: F3 all day — the GRIB shows no more
F3 with some rain, nothing more
Calm — storms kill the wind
why: Thunderstorm gusts are local and short; forecasts and GRIBs give only the background wind.

q: By 10:00 the cumulus over the mainland mountains is already towering high and darkening. What does it mean for your day?
a: Thunderstorms likely — be in port early
o: Fair weather — puffy cloud is a good sign
Fog will form by the evening
A Meltemi will start tonight
why: Cumulus growing tall by mid-morning signals afternoon thunderstorms.

q: A low, dark roll of cloud with a line of white water beneath it is racing towards you. What do you do?
a: Reduce sail now, before it hits
o: Slow down and sound fog signals
Nothing — it is only rain
Shake out a reef for the breeze
why: A roll cloud with white water under it is a squall line — minutes away.

q: What is forming, and will the breeze clear it?
a: Sea fog — it can persist despite the wind
o: Radiation fog — the breeze will clear it
Heat haze — it will lift by noon
Sea mist — it always clears by noon
why: Advection fog: warm moist air cooled over a cold sea; wind does not disperse it.

fig.title: Northern Adriatic, May
lines: Sea still cold after the winter

q: Your passage is 20 miles along the coast. What do you do?
a: Wait — it should burn off by mid-morning
o: Cancel — this fog will last all day
Leave now — it is the same at sea all day
Leave now and steer by radar alone
why: Radiation fog forms over land on clear calm nights and clears as the sun warms it.

fig.title: Marina, October, 06:30
lines: Thick fog in the harbour, blue sky above

q: What do you expect overnight?
a: Fog or mist forming over the sea
o: A dry, clear night with good visibility
A strong land breeze
Heavy thunderstorms with hail
why: Moist air at its dew point flowing over colder sea will form advection fog.

q: When are you most likely to meet sea fog in the northern Adriatic?
a: Spring, while the sea is still cold
o: Mid-August, at the height of summer
Only when the Bora is blowing
Every summer afternoon at 16:00
why: Sea fog needs warm moist air over a sea still cold from winter.

q: What does the swell tell you?
a: A distant system — swell runs ahead
o: A sea breeze will start up within the hour
Settled weather for days to come
It is the wake of a passing ship
why: Swell travels faster than the weather that made it and is an early warning.

lines: Long, low swell from the SW, building

q: Where will you spend a comfortable night?
a: B — tucked away from the swell
o: A — sheltered from the north wind
C — open to the south
Any — the wind is light
why: Swell can make an anchorage untenable even in light wind; hide from the swell direction.

fig.note: Wind N 2 · SW swell 1.5 m tonight

q: The Meltemi blew F7 for three days and stopped at dawn. You plan to leave Naxos northwards this morning. What do you expect?
a: A big leftover sea for some hours
o: Flat calm water as soon as you leave
The wind back within the hour
Fog from the cooled sea
why: The sea takes hours to go down after a long blow.

q: How do you plan the day's passage?
a: Sail early, shelter and rest at midday
o: Sail in the midday heat, when it is calm
Skip hats and shade — it is only a day
Ration water to make it last
why: Avoid the midday sun, drink plenty and keep the crew in shade.

q: What do you decide?
a: Stay and wait for the wind to ease
o: Go — it is a downwind run
Go with full sail to be quick
Go, but reef down if anyone feels ill
why: Rough sea, strong gusts and a mostly new crew on an open crossing: wait for a better window.

q: You must pick a night anchorage. Which one?
a: B — sheltered now and after the shift
o: A — handy for tomorrow's leg west
C — calm now, behind the island
Any — the wind backs only after midnight
why: Choose shelter for the wind you will have overnight, not only the wind you have now.
